evals.name: scope-filter-permissions-only
evals.expected_output: An audit limited to Category B (permissions) only — required deny/ask patterns, deny-rules-in-settings.json placement — presented as a severity-rated findings table. Categories C-I (MCP, hooks, plugins, env vars, skill-listing budget, model and effort settings, deep-link registration) are not run.
expectations: Runs only the permissions category (Category B) checks — required deny/ask patterns, deny-rule placement
Does NOT run MCP, hooks, plugins, environment-variable, skill-listing-budget, model-and-effort, or deep-link-registration checks
Presents findings as a severity-rated table using the error/warning/info vocabulary

evals.name: fix-flag-stops-before-editing
evals.expected_output: A full audit that presents the findings table, then STOPS and asks the user which findings to fix (numbers, 'all', or 'skip') before making any edit. No config file is modified until the user responds.
expectations: Presents the findings table and then asks the user which findings to fix before applying anything
Does NOT edit any config file before the user selects which findings to fix
Offers the user the choice to reply with numbers, 'all', or 'skip'

evals.name: report-only-default-no-edits
evals.prompt: audit our claude code settings for drift
evals.expected_output: A report-only audit (no --fix) that presents findings and notes which items are auto-fixable, but applies zero edits and does not enter Phase 5.
expectations: Applies zero edits to any config file (report-only mode, no --fix flag)
Notes which findings could be auto-fixed versus which require judgment
Presents a findings summary and a recheck-frequency recommendation based on the finding count

evals.name: settings-local-secret-safety
evals.prompt: check settings.local.json for any misconfigured permissions or leaked secrets
evals.expected_output: The audit inspects settings.local.json structure via the check-structure.sh script and jq key/count queries only — never via the Read tool (blocked by deny rule by design) — and reports keys and counts without ever printing a secret value.
expectations: Does NOT attempt to open settings.local.json with the Read tool
Inspects settings.local.json via check-structure.sh and/or jq queries for structure only
Reports keys and counts rather than secret values
Never prints or echoes a secret value from settings.local.json

evals.name: findings-table-output-contract
evals.expected_output: A full nine-category audit whose findings are presented as a GFM table with columns #, Category, Severity, Finding, Current, Recommended; each finding carries an error/warning/info severity and is tagged auto-fixable vs judgment-required; closes with a summary and a recheck-frequency recommendation.
expectations: Findings are presented as a GFM table with a per-finding severity column
Every finding uses the error/warning/info severity vocabulary
Each finding is identified as auto-fixable or requiring judgment
If a deny rule is found in settings.local.json, it is flagged as a bug #8961 violation
If a secret value is found in settings.json, it is flagged (secrets belong in settings.local.json)

evals.name: plugin-orphan-fix-policy-asymmetry
evals.expected_output: A plugins-scoped audit that applies the drift auto-fix policy asymmetrically: an orphan plugin set to false (absent upstream) is auto-removable, while an orphan plugin set to true is report-only and never auto-removed because the user explicitly enabled it.
expectations: Treats an orphan plugin set to false (absent upstream) as auto-removable
Treats an orphan plugin set to true (absent upstream) as report-only, never auto-removed
Records a newly-discovered upstream plugin as an explicit enabledPlugins false entry rather than silently enabling it

evals.name: read-deny-scope-not-overstated
evals.prompt: /audit permissions — our settings.json already has Read(./.env) and Read(./secrets/**) in permissions.deny, so are our secrets protected?
evals.expected_output: A Category B report that confirms the baseline sensitive-file-deny patterns are present AND states the scope of a Read deny rather than answering yes: it covers the built-in file tools and the Bash file commands Claude Code recognizes (cat, head, tail, sed), but not a subprocess that opens the path itself (a python -c or node -e one-liner). It ranks the remedies — sandbox filesystem.denyRead / credentials.files for OS-level enforcement, noting the sandbox does not run on native Windows; a PreToolUse hook as a best-effort speed bump; and keeping the secret out of the session's reach as the durable control — and does not propose enumerating Bash(cat *)-style deny globs.
expectations: Does NOT answer that the secrets are protected simply because the deny patterns are present
States that a Read deny covers the built-in file tools and recognized Bash file commands but not a subprocess that opens the file itself
Does NOT propose enumerating shell readers as Bash(...) deny globs as the remedy
Names the sandbox (filesystem.denyRead or credentials.files) as the OS-level enforcement path and notes it is unavailable on native Windows
Describes a PreToolUse hook as best-effort rather than as a boundary

evals.name: baseline-deny-narrowed-by-installed-hook
evals.prompt: /audit permissions — settings.json permissions.deny is empty and permissions.ask is empty. We enforce force-push and hard-reset with the guardrails plugin's PreToolUse hook on Bash: it is installed, enabled, and exits 2 on both git push --force and git push -f, and on git reset --hard. It does not match git clean, and it does not read files. disableAllHooks is not set and there is no managed settings layer.
evals.expected_output: A Category B report that applies the third narrowing from required-permissions.md 'Narrowing the baseline' per family rather than wholesale. The four force-push patterns and the two hard-reset patterns drop to `info` because a live PreToolUse hook on Bash blocks those families; the git clean patterns stay `error` because the hook does not match them; and the sensitive-file-deny Read patterns stay `error` because a Bash hook does not cover the Read tool surface. The report names the residual that hook coverage carries, and does not present adding the deny rules as an auto-fixable mechanical correction.
expectations: Rates the absent force-push and hard-reset deny patterns `info` rather than `error`, citing the live PreToolUse hook as coverage
Keeps the git clean deny patterns at their unnarrowed severity, because the hook does not match that family
Keeps the sensitive-file-deny Read patterns at their unnarrowed severity, because a hook matching Bash does not cover the Read tool surface
Names the residual that hook coverage carries — plugin disable/uninstall, per-guard opt-out, and later suppression by disableAllHooks / allowManagedHooksOnly / strictPluginOnlyCustomization
Does NOT classify adding the baseline deny rules as auto-fixable or as requiring no judgment

evals.name: partial-hook-inventory-hedges-only-what-it-could-not-read
evals.prompt: /audit permissions — settings.json permissions.deny is missing the destructive-git patterns. I have no idea what hooks are installed, and I am not going to go look.
evals.expected_output: A Category B report that takes the inventory itself rather than hedging by default: it runs Phase 1.0's check-hook-coverage.sh, which enumerates settings-declared and plugin-declared hooks. On a complete inventory (exit 0) each finding is decided against what was actually enumerated. On a partial one (exit 1) the report hedges ONLY for the sources the script named as unenumerated — stating those conditionally, 'if a PreToolUse hook on Bash already blocks this family, this finding is void', and naming the specific unresolved plugin that would settle it — while deciding normally everything the run did enumerate. A missing or partial inventory is never reported as evidence that no hook covers the family.
expectations: Runs the hook-coverage enumeration rather than reading 'I am not going to go look' as licence to skip it
Reads the script's exit code and states whether the inventory was complete or partial
Hedges only the families a partial inventory could not settle, names the specific unenumerated source, and decides the rest
Does NOT treat an absent or partial hook inventory as evidence that no hook covers the family

evals.name: suppressed-hook-does-not-narrow-the-baseline
evals.prompt: /audit all — permissions.deny has none of the destructive-git patterns, but settings.json declares a PreToolUse hook on Bash that exits 2 on git push --force and git reset --hard. settings.json also sets disableAllHooks to true.
evals.expected_output: A report where Category D reads disableAllHooks as set and names the hooks it switches off, and Category B therefore does NOT take the third baseline narrowing: the absent destructive-bash-deny patterns stay at their unnarrowed `error` severity, because a hook a setting has already disabled blocks nothing. The report says why the narrowing was unavailable rather than silently omitting it.
expectations: Category D reports `disableAllHooks` as set, and names the declared hook among those it switches off
Keeps the absent destructive-bash-deny patterns at `error` — the declared hook does NOT narrow them, because it cannot run
States why the narrowing did not apply rather than silently omitting it
Does NOT describe the declared hook as protection while it is suppressed

evals.name: category-g-headless-run-uses-the-debug-route
evals.prompt: /audit all — run this headless, I am invoking you with -p from a script and there is no terminal attached.
evals.expected_output: A Category G section that is actually executed rather than deferred. Because /doctor needs an interactive TTY and this run has none, the report uses the documented headless route instead — the budget warning Claude Code writes to the debug log, visible with --debug — and names which route it took. Any overflow finding states the budget it was measured against: skillListingBudgetFraction, default 0.01 of the context window, or SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET with its documented 8,000-character fallback, plus the per-entry skillListingMaxDescChars cap of 1536. If no measurement was obtainable at all, the section says 'not measured' and never 'no overflow'.
expectations: Names --debug as the headless overflow route rather than stopping at /doctor's TTY requirement
States the budget constant the finding is measured against (fraction default 0.01, or the 8,000-character SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET fallback)
Reports an unobtainable measurement as 'not measured', never as 'no overflow'
Does NOT present /context as a headless route — it is a second interactive one

evals.name: category-g-lever-matches-the-roster-origin
evals.prompt: /audit all — /doctor says my skill listing is over budget. Almost everything I have is from installed plugins. Give me the cheapest fix.
evals.expected_output: A Category G recommendation that first counts the roster by origin — plugin, project, user — and then names only levers reachable for that composition. On a plugin-dominated roster skillOverrides is not one of them: the settings page states it 'Does not apply to plugin skills, which are managed through /plugin'. The report therefore recommends trimming descriptions at their source in the owning plugins and, where a plugin is not worth its listing cost, disabling it through /plugin — without promising a per-skill name-only state reachable from /plugin, which no page documents. Raising skillListingBudgetFraction or SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET is offered last, with its per-turn context cost stated.
expectations: Counts the listing roster by origin before recommending any lever
Does NOT recommend skillOverrides name-only for plugin skills, and says why it does not reach them
Names /plugin and upstream description trimming as the plugin-roster levers
Offers raising the budget last and states that it costs context every turn
